title: Alternative Paths
hook: The path that happened can erase the paths that were still real yesterday.
counterintuition: A good outcome does not prove the choice was safe, and a bad outcome does not prove the choice was foolish. Judge the live paths that existed before the result arrived.
tryThisNow: Before praising or blaming one decision today, write three live alternatives that existed before the outcome was known.
keyTakeaway: Judge a decision by the real paths available at the time, not only by the path that became visible.

breakdown.fastRead:
The visitor badge lies beside the emergency dispatch script while Susan reviews a call that ended well. The ambulance found the patient in time. The room wants to call the shortcut brilliant. Susan writes alternative paths beside the badge.

The outcome is only one path. Other live paths existed when the choice was made: a locked gate, a wrong address, a second call, a radio failure. Once the good result appears, those paths fade.

Visible history is not the whole risk.

The correction is to rebuild the decision before the result. What could have happened then? Which paths were likely, costly, or survivable?
breakdown.deepRead:
The visitor badge in Susan's dispatch review belongs to a trainee who skipped two script checks during a cardiac call. The team arrived fast, and the patient survived. The shortcut now looks like judgment. Susan marks alternative paths risk because the same shortcut could have ended with a missed allergy note, a locked stairwell, or the wrong unit sent to the address.

Alternative paths are the routes reality could have taken from the same starting point. After the fact, only one route is visible, and the visible route starts to feel natural. The decision looks cleaner than it was because the branches that did not happen no longer demand attention.

The missing branch still matters.

Craig sees the same issue in travel insurance pricing. A mild hurricane season makes last year's cheap policy look smart. The sample tray of claim categories sits beside the pricing sheet, and the team wants to cut reserves again. Craig writes Russian roulette risk on the tray because one safe spin does not prove the chamber was empty. He prices the next policy from storm paths that could have happened, not only from the calm season that did.

This is not regret for every ghost outcome. Many imagined paths are fantasy. The discipline is narrower: recover the alternatives that were live at the time, given the information, constraints, and probabilities people actually faced. Then judge the choice against that set.

A result tells you what happened, not everything that was risked.
breakdown.fullRead:
The inspection tag on Lucy's podcast ad renewal has a red corner where the host missed a required disclosure line. The campaign still sold well. The marketing lead says the risk was overblown because nothing bad happened. Lucy points to the visible history problem: the audience did not complain, the regulator did not notice, and the brand did not pull out. Those are facts, but they are not the only paths that were open.

Alternative paths matter because life does not show the full tree after one branch wins. A risky move can survive and look wise. A careful move can fail and look timid. The visible result is loud, while the paths not taken are silent.

Russian roulette is the hard image for this. A person who survives one pull of the trigger can say the outcome was good. That does not make the act prudent. Nassim Nicholas Taleb used this kind of example to show how visible history can flatter risk takers. Survival is real, but it is not the same as safety.

What was possible before you knew what happened?

Lucy asks that question beside the inspection tag. The disclosure miss could have gone unnoticed, as it did. It also could have triggered a listener complaint, a sponsor review, or a contract penalty. Those paths were not fantasy. They were live consequences tied to the same decision. The renewal now includes a compliance check before creative approval, even though the last campaign ended well.

You can feel this in a university lab result meeting. You are holding a floor plan while Joel reviews a successful shortcut around a temperature-controlled storage room. The samples survived. The publication moved forward. Joel must decide whether Taleb risk is being ignored: the live alternative path included a freezer alarm, a spoiled batch, and a lost grant window.

The same correction applies after failure. A charity donor campaign may miss its target after a careful plan, and the room may call the plan bad. Vanessa has to ask what other paths were live before the weather turned, the payment system stalled, and a local news story crowded out the appeal. Failure can reveal weak design, but it can also reveal a bad draw from a sensible set of options.

Reconstructing paths is not hindsight theater. Do not invent heroic alternatives nobody could have known. Do not imagine perfect information after the result. Use only the options, warnings, and probabilities that were available at the decision point. The question is not what you can dream up now. It is what the choice exposed you to then.

Judge a decision by the real paths available at the time, not only by the path that became visible.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Alternative paths protect readers from judging risk by one visible result. The skill is to reconstruct live options before praise, blame, or repetition.

reviewCards.front: A risky shortcut works. What should you reconstruct?
reviewCards.back: Reconstruct the live paths that could have happened from the same decision, including downside paths that stayed hidden.

reviewCards.front: Why can a good outcome mislead risk judgment?
reviewCards.back: It shows the path that happened, not the other paths the choice exposed you to.

reviewCards.front: What is the Russian roulette lesson for decisions?
reviewCards.back: Survival from a risky act does not prove the act was safe.

reviewCards.front: How do you avoid fantasy hindsight?
reviewCards.back: Use only alternatives, warnings, and probabilities that were available before the outcome.

reviewCards.front: What is the core correction for alternative paths?
reviewCards.back: Judge the decision by the live paths at the time, not only by the visible result.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to judge decisions by exposure, not only by outcome. The practical habit is to rebuild live paths before praise, blame, or repetition.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a shortcut works, then I will list the plausible paths where it failed before making it standard.
If a plan fails, then I will rebuild the information and risks available before calling it foolish.
If someone says nothing bad happened, then I will ask what bad paths were live.
If a result looks brilliant or terrible, then I will separate decision quality from outcome luck.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, pick one recent win or miss and write the three live paths that did not happen.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review a near miss and score the decision from the risks present before the outcome was known.
